opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, Copilot was one of the clearest lessons I've had that latency isn't just an engineering metric. It's part of what the product *is*.

When we started working with GitHub on Codex powering code completion, the natural instinct was to ask, "How do we get the smartest possible suggestion?" And very quickly you realize that's the wrong question if the answer shows up too late. A developer is typing, they're in flow, and if the suggestion arrives after they've already written the next few characters, it doesn't matter how good it is. It's noise. Worse, it's a distraction.

So there's this real tradeoff between model capability and speed, and the right point on that curve depends on the interaction. For inline completion you're competing with the speed of human thought and typing. You have maybe a few hundred milliseconds before the moment passes. That pushed us toward a smaller, faster model than we might have chosen if we'd only looked at benchmark quality. A slightly less capable model that answers instantly often beats a smarter one that makes you wait.

The other thing it taught me is that latency changes behavior. When suggestions are fast, people start relying on them in a different way. They type a little and pause, expecting the tool to fill in the rest. It becomes a collaborator rather than something you consult. That shift only happens below a certain latency threshold. Above it, people treat it like a search box, and the whole relationship changes.

There's a lot of invisible work behind that too: caching, deciding when to trigger a request at all, cancelling stale requests when someone keeps typing, streaming, and getting the context into the prompt efficiently. None of that shows up in a demo, but it's the difference between something that feels magical and something that feels clunky.

I think that lesson generalizes. As models get more capable, it's tempting to assume intelligence is the only thing that matters. But the experience is intelligence multiplied by responsiveness, and if either goes to zero, the product does too. Now that we're building systems that can think for a long time and run agentically, it's the same principle in a different form: match how long the system takes to how the person is actually working. Sometimes that means instant. Sometimes it means going off for an hour and coming back with something great. The mistake is getting that mismatch wrong.

r001.rationale: It says a suggestion that arrives after the developer has moved on is noise or a distraction, even if it is otherwise good.

r002.rationale: It describes balancing model capability against speed and choosing a smaller, faster model when a smarter one would arrive too late.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: You know, Copilot was really the first time we shipped a model into a surface where people were using it hundreds of times an hour, not a few times a day. And that changes everything. With a chat product, if you wait three seconds for an answer, that's fine, you're having a conversation. But when someone's typing code and a suggestion is supposed to appear as a ghost completion, if it shows up 800 milliseconds late, they've already moved on. They've typed the next character, and now the suggestion is wrong, or it's stale, or it just feels like the tool is fighting them.

So the thing we learned, and I think this was genuinely surprising to a lot of us on the research side, is that latency isn't a nice-to-have on top of quality. It's part of quality. A slightly dumber model that responds in 200 milliseconds will get accepted more often than a smarter one that takes a second and a half. People's acceptance rate was incredibly sensitive to this. We'd see curves where you'd shave off a couple hundred milliseconds and the usage would jump in a way that no amount of improvement to the model's raw benchmark score would give you.

And it forced a bunch of really unglamorous engineering. Things like, how do you cancel a request the moment the user types another key, so you're not wasting compute on a completion nobody will see. How do you stream the first few tokens and decide whether this is even worth showing. How do you structure the context window so you're not re-sending the whole file every keystroke. We had to think about the model, the serving stack, and the editor plugin as one system, because the user experiences them as one thing.

The broader lesson I took away is that when you're putting a model into a tool people use continuously, you have to design for the human's loop, not the model's loop. The human has a rhythm, and your job is to fit inside it. If you do that, the model feels like an extension of your own thinking. If you don't, it feels like an interruption, no matter how good the answer is. That mindset carried into a lot of what we built afterward.

r001.rationale: The response says a late suggestion can be stale or wrong and that users may accept a faster, less capable model over a slower, smarter one.

r002.rationale: It describes the speed-versus-quality tradeoff, but does not state the model-selection objective as choosing the smartest model that meets a latency constraint.

astra-6.text:
Copilot really drove home that latency is part of whether a product works at all. When you’re writing code, you have a thought in your head and you’re moving quickly. If a suggestion arrives after you’ve already started typing the next thing, it doesn’t matter how good it is—you’ve moved on. But if it arrives at the right moment, it can feel like a natural extension of what you’re doing.

So you can’t think about model quality in isolation. You have to think about the whole experience: how useful is the suggestion, and can we deliver it while it’s still useful? Sometimes a faster response is more valuable than a better response that comes too late.

r001.rationale: It says that even a good suggestion is no use if it arrives after the user has moved on.

r002.rationale: It describes balancing usefulness and speed, but does not state that Copilot should choose the smartest model that meets a latency constraint.

sol-6.1.text:
One of the big lessons was that latency isn’t just an engineering metric—it changes what the product can be. With Copilot, you’re trying to offer a suggestion while someone is thinking about their code. If it arrives too late, they’ve already moved on, and even a good suggestion can become an interruption.

So you can’t think about model quality in isolation. You have to think about whether the suggestion is useful at the moment it appears. A faster response can make the interaction feel fundamentally different: you stay in your flow, and the tool feels like an extension of what you’re doing. That made latency a core part of the product design.

r001.rationale: It says even a good suggestion can become an interruption if it arrives after the user has moved on.

r002.rationale: It says model quality and latency both matter, but does not identify choosing the smartest model that meets a latency constraint as the selection objective.
